judge.reasoning:
The report addresses reasonable high-level demographics (income, education, age, labor force, commute) that broadly matter for a fast-casual vegan concept, so section relevance is moderate. However, several issues cap the scores.

GEOGRAPHIC GRANULARITY MISMATCH (major): The brief explicitly asks for "dense urban neighborhoods... near gyms, yoga studios, and office districts with lunchtime foot traffic." The report analyzes only three enormous COUNTIES (Los Angeles, Orange, San Diego — 9.8M, 3.1M, 3.3M residents). At this resolution the report cannot help the owner "pick a location" — it cannot distinguish a foot-traffic-heavy office/gym corridor from a car-dependent suburb. A useful site-selection report needed ZIP- or tract-level analysis. This is the single biggest limitation and heavily drags down overall_quality. Note also "zip_count": 3 while the data are clearly counties — an internal inconsistency.

TOOL SELECTION GAPS: For this ideal customer (health-conscious millennials/Gen Z, fitness enthusiasts, office workers) the agent missed the most decisive metrics: age BREAKDOWN isolating the 20-39 cohort (only median age is shown, which at ~37 obscures the target segment), daytime/employment density or worker inflow (the true lunch-traffic driver, not resident labor-force participation), population/commercial density, and walkability/transit-to-work share. Commute TIME is a weak proxy and arguably mismatched — the narrative claims "shorter commutes... support grab-and-go," yet commute time alone says nothing about pedestrian lunch traffic. So tool selection is mediocre with notable mismatches.

NARRATIVE QUALITY: The prose is fluent but generic and somewhat data-detached. It repeatedly asserts the market "skews younger" and "over-indexes on plant-based eating" while the shown median ages (~37) and county-level data don't substantiate segment specificity. It restates section descriptions rather than delivering sharp, location-specific, actionable recommendations. No concrete neighborhood guidance despite the brief. Reads like polished filler.

DATA PLAUSIBILITY: Values are largely believable for SoCal counties — median incomes ~$97K-112K, college-educated ~40%, labor force ~67-68%, commute ~25-28 min are all reasonable. The summary median income of ~$101K and median age ~38.6 are plausible aggregates. Minor concern: six-figure-household shares (44-56%) in the bubble chart are on the high side but not absurd for these metros; still credible. Solid here.

VISUALIZATION: Bar charts are appropriate for the categorical geography comparisons, and the multi-dimensional bubble chart (income% vs education% vs population) is a fitting choice. However, several bars carry a redundant/incorrect 'percentage' field equal to the raw value (e.g., median age 36.5 labeled as percentage 36.5), and distributions (e.g., age or income spread) would have been more insightful than single median bars. Appropriate but unpolished.

Overall: a coherent, presentable-looking but not decision-ready report — the county-level geography fundamentally undercuts its stated site-selection purpose, hence a middling overall score.
